quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L131-Q1-0] Explicitly
pairs.value: Stated directly and specifically, leaving no room for doubt.

pairs.key: [L131-Q1-1] Implicitly
pairs.value: Understood without being directly stated.

pairs.key: [L131-Q1-2] Exclusively
pairs.value: Limited to only the thing mentioned, with nothing else included.

pairs.key: [L131-Q1-3] Inclusively
pairs.value: Covering everything within a stated range, with nothing left out.

quests.hint: Two of these describe how directly or indirectly something is expressed. Two describe how wide or narrow a scope is.
quests.explanation: Explicitly and implicitly are opposites describing whether something is directly stated or only understood. Exclusively and inclusively are different — both are about scope, one narrowing to just one thing, one covering everything within a range.

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L131-Q2-0] This clause applies exclusively to full-time employees.
pairs.value: This rule covers only full-time employees, and no one else.

pairs.key: [L131-Q2-1] Part-time staff are implicitly excluded, though not named directly.
pairs.value: Part-time workers are left out by clear implication, even though the clause doesn't name them specifically.

pairs.key: [L131-Q2-2] The agreement explicitly states a notice period of thirty days.
pairs.value: The contract directly and clearly specifies a thirty-day notice requirement.

pairs.key: [L131-Q2-3] This applies to all days inclusively, including weekends and holidays.
pairs.value: This rule counts every single day within the range, weekends and holidays included.

quests.hint: Each sentence adds a precise detail to the same explanation of a contract clause.
quests.explanation: The first sentence states who the clause covers, and the second clarifies who it doesn't, without naming them. The third states a clear requirement, while the fourth is different — it describes how broadly a different rule applies.

quests.instruction: Match each version with its precise meaning.

pairs.key: [L131-Q3-0] Employees must give thirty days' notice before resigning.
pairs.value: A worker who wants to resign is required to inform the company at least a month in advance.

pairs.key: [L131-Q3-1] Employees are encouraged to give thirty days' notice before resigning.
pairs.value: A worker who wants to resign is asked, but not required, to inform the company a month in advance.

pairs.key: [L131-Q3-2] Employees gave thirty days' notice before resigning.
pairs.value: In this case, workers already informed the company a month in advance before leaving.

pairs.key: [L131-Q3-3] Employees rarely give thirty days' notice before resigning.
pairs.value: In practice, workers usually do not inform the company a full month in advance before leaving.

quests.hint: These four sentences look almost identical but differ in one small, important way — whether something is required, suggested, already done, or rarely done.
quests.explanation: The first states an outright requirement, must. The second softens that to encouragement, not a rule. The third describes something already completed, in the past. The fourth is different from all three — it describes how rarely this actually happens in practice.
quests.paragraphTopic: Precise paraphrasing of a workplace policy

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L132-Q1-0] Assert
pairs.value: To state something firmly as true.

pairs.key: [L132-Q1-1] Concede
pairs.value: To admit that a point made by an opposing view has some validity.

pairs.key: [L132-Q1-2] Refute
pairs.value: To prove that a claim or argument is wrong.

pairs.key: [L132-Q1-3] Qualify
pairs.value: To limit or adjust a claim so it isn't stated too broadly.

quests.hint: One means stating something firmly, one means admitting a point, one means disproving a claim, and one means narrowing a claim.
quests.explanation: Assert and refute are opposite moves in an argument, one stating a claim, one disproving one. Concede and qualify are different — both soften an argument somewhat, one by admitting a fair point, one by narrowing the claim's scope.

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L132-Q2-0] The essay asserts that remote work improves productivity.
pairs.value: The essay directly claims that working from home increases how much gets done.

pairs.key: [L132-Q2-1] It concedes that this may not hold true for every industry.
pairs.value: It admits that this claim might not apply equally to all types of work.

pairs.key: [L132-Q2-2] The writer then refutes the common claim that remote workers are less accountable.
pairs.value: The writer goes on to disprove the widespread idea that people working from home are less responsible.

pairs.key: [L132-Q2-3] The conclusion qualifies the argument, applying it mainly to knowledge-based roles.
pairs.value: The ending narrows the claim, saying it mostly applies to jobs based on information and expertise.

quests.hint: Each sentence describes a different move the same essay makes as it builds its argument.
quests.explanation: The first sentence states the essay's main claim, and the second admits a limitation to it. The third describes the essay disproving an opposing view, while the fourth is different — it describes how the conclusion narrows the original claim.
quests.paragraphTopic: How an essay builds and limits its argument

quests.instruction: Match each version with its precise meaning.

pairs.key: [L132-Q3-0] Remote work always improves productivity.
pairs.value: This claims that working from home improves output in every single case, without exception.

pairs.key: [L132-Q3-1] Remote work can improve productivity.
pairs.value: This claims that working from home has the potential to improve output, though not guaranteed.

pairs.key: [L132-Q3-2] Remote work improved productivity in this case.
pairs.value: This claims that, in this particular instance, working from home did increase output.

pairs.key: [L132-Q3-3] Remote work rarely improves productivity.
pairs.value: This claims that working from home usually fails to increase output.

quests.hint: These four sentences look almost identical but differ in a small but important way — how certain and how general each claim really is.
quests.explanation: The first claims something happens in every case, always. The second only claims it's possible, can. The third describes one specific instance, in the past. The fourth is different from all three — it claims the opposite usually happens, rarely.
quests.paragraphTopic: Precise paraphrasing of a claim's certainty

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L133-Q1-0] Required
pairs.value: Must be done; not optional.

pairs.key: [L133-Q1-1] Suggested
pairs.value: Offered as helpful advice, though not compulsory.

pairs.key: [L133-Q1-2] Discretionary
pairs.value: Left up to individual judgment or choice.

pairs.key: [L133-Q1-3] Deprecated
pairs.value: Still working for now, but officially discouraged and likely to be removed later.

quests.hint: One is a firm requirement, one is friendly advice, one is left to choice, and one is on its way out.
quests.explanation: Required and suggested both relate to what you should do, one mandatory, one merely advised. Discretionary and deprecated are different — one is entirely up to personal choice, one is still usable but officially on its way out.

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L133-Q2-0] Setting an API key is required before making any requests.
pairs.value: You must set up an API key before you can send any requests at all.

pairs.key: [L133-Q2-1] Using a config file is suggested, but not strictly necessary.
pairs.value: Using a configuration file is a good idea, though it isn't required.

pairs.key: [L133-Q2-2] Logging level is discretionary and can be adjusted freely.
pairs.value: You can choose the logging level yourself, based on your own preference.

pairs.key: [L133-Q2-3] The old authentication method is deprecated and may be removed in a future release.
pairs.value: The older way of logging in still works for now, but it's officially discouraged and could be taken away later.

quests.hint: Each sentence describes a different requirement level in the same piece of documentation.
quests.explanation: The first sentence describes a firm requirement, and the second describes friendly, optional advice. The third describes something left entirely to choice, while the fourth is different — it describes something still working but being phased out.

quests.instruction: Match each version with its precise meaning.

pairs.key: [L133-Q3-0] You must configure the timeout setting.
pairs.value: Configuring the timeout is not optional; it has to be done.

pairs.key: [L133-Q3-1] You may want to configure the timeout setting.
pairs.value: Configuring the timeout is a reasonable idea, though entirely up to you.

pairs.key: [L133-Q3-2] You no longer need to configure the timeout setting.
pairs.value: Configuring the timeout used to be necessary, but it isn't anymore.

pairs.key: [L133-Q3-3] You should avoid configuring the timeout setting manually.
pairs.value: Manually configuring the timeout is discouraged, and doing so could cause a problem.

quests.hint: These four sentences look almost identical but differ in a small but important way — whether something is required, optional, no longer needed, or discouraged.
quests.explanation: The first states an outright requirement, must. The second softens that to a suggestion, may want to. The third describes something no longer necessary, though it once was. The fourth is different from all three — it actively discourages an action.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L134-Q1-0] Projected
pairs.value: Expected or forecasted for the future, based on current trends.

pairs.key: [L134-Q1-1] Actual
pairs.value: What really happened, as opposed to what was expected.

pairs.key: [L134-Q1-2] Estimated
pairs.value: Roughly calculated, without being fully precise.

pairs.key: [L134-Q1-3] Realized
pairs.value: Actually achieved or converted into real profit or loss.

quests.hint: Two of these describe numbers based on forecasting or rough calculation, and two describe numbers that actually happened.
quests.explanation: Projected and estimated both describe forecasted or roughly calculated numbers, before the real outcome is known. Actual and realized are different — both describe real outcomes, one general, one specifically about profit that was actually converted.

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L134-Q2-0] Projected revenue for the quarter was $2 million.
pairs.value: The company expected to bring in about two million dollars for the quarter, based on forecasts.

pairs.key: [L134-Q2-1] Actual revenue came in slightly higher, at $2.3 million.
pairs.value: What the company really earned ended up a bit above that, at $2.3 million.

pairs.key: [L134-Q2-2] Estimated costs were harder to pin down due to supply issues.
pairs.value: Roughly calculated expenses were less certain because of problems with supplies.

pairs.key: [L134-Q2-3] Realized gains from the investment portfolio offset some of the shortfall.
pairs.value: Profits that were actually converted from investments helped make up for part of the gap.

quests.hint: Each sentence adds a different kind of financial figure to the same quarterly report.
quests.explanation: The first sentence gives a forecasted number, and the second gives the real result that followed. The third describes a rougher, less certain figure, while the fourth is different — it describes profit that was genuinely converted, offsetting other numbers.

quests.instruction: Match each version with its precise meaning.

pairs.key: [L134-Q3-0] Revenue is projected to reach $3 million next quarter.
pairs.value: The company forecasts it will earn about three million dollars next quarter, though this hasn't happened yet.

pairs.key: [L134-Q3-1] Revenue reached $3 million last quarter.
pairs.value: The company actually earned three million dollars in the quarter that already ended.

pairs.key: [L134-Q3-2] Revenue is estimated at roughly $3 million for last quarter.
pairs.value: The company's earnings for the completed quarter are believed to be about three million, though the exact figure isn't confirmed yet.

pairs.key: [L134-Q3-3] Revenue exceeded $3 million last quarter.
pairs.value: The company's confirmed earnings for the completed quarter were more than three million.

quests.hint: These four sentences look almost identical but differ in a small but important way — whether a number is forecasted, confirmed, estimated, or definitely exceeded.
quests.explanation: The first is a forecast for the future, projected. The second is a confirmed result from the past, reached. The third is a rough calculation for a period already over, estimated. The fourth is different from all three — it confirms the actual number went beyond the figure mentioned.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L135-Q1-0] Contraindicated
pairs.value: Specifically advised against because it could cause harm in a particular situation.

pairs.key: [L135-Q1-1] Advisable
pairs.value: Sensible or wise to do, though not strictly required.

pairs.key: [L135-Q1-2] Prohibited
pairs.value: Not allowed under any circumstances.

pairs.key: [L135-Q1-3] Permissible
pairs.value: Allowed; not against the rules.

quests.hint: One is specifically advised against, one is simply wise, one is banned outright, and one is allowed.
quests.explanation: Contraindicated and prohibited both describe things to avoid, though contraindicated is a specific medical warning, while prohibited is a firm ban of any kind. Advisable and permissible are different — one is a positive suggestion, one is simply allowed, without necessarily being recommended.

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L135-Q2-0] This medication is contraindicated for patients with liver disease.
pairs.value: This medicine specifically shouldn't be used by patients who have liver disease, because of the risk.

pairs.key: [L135-Q2-1] It's advisable to take it with food to reduce stomach upset.
pairs.value: Taking it with food is a sensible idea, since it can help avoid stomach discomfort.

pairs.key: [L135-Q2-2] Mixing it with alcohol is strictly prohibited.
pairs.value: Combining it with alcohol is not allowed under any circumstances.

pairs.key: [L135-Q2-3] Occasional use of pain relievers alongside it is permissible.
pairs.value: Using pain relievers with it now and then is allowed.

quests.hint: Each sentence describes a different level of medical guidance for the same medication.
quests.explanation: The first sentence gives a specific medical warning, and the second gives helpful, non-mandatory advice. The third gives a strict ban, while the fourth is different — it confirms something is simply allowed, without being either advised or banned.

quests.instruction: Match each version with its precise meaning.

pairs.key: [L135-Q3-0] Patients with liver disease should not take this medication.
pairs.value: This medicine is unsafe for patients who have liver disease and should be avoided by them.

pairs.key: [L135-Q3-1] Patients with liver disease may need a lower dose of this medication.
pairs.value: This medicine might still be usable for patients with liver disease, but possibly at a reduced amount.

pairs.key: [L135-Q3-2] Patients with liver disease have taken this medication safely.
pairs.value: In practice, some patients with liver disease have used this medicine without a problem.

pairs.key: [L135-Q3-3] Patients with liver disease are rarely prescribed this medication.
pairs.value: Doctors don't often give this medicine to patients who have liver disease, though it does happen sometimes.

quests.hint: These four sentences look almost identical but differ in a small but important way — whether something is unsafe, possibly reduced, already done, or simply uncommon.
quests.explanation: The first states a clear warning against use, should not. The second allows for a modified, safer option, may need a lower dose. The third describes something that has already happened safely, in practice. The fourth is different from all three — it describes how uncommon this is, without saying it's unsafe.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L136-Q1-0] Mandated
pairs.value: Required by law or official authority.

pairs.key: [L136-Q1-1] Voluntary
pairs.value: Done by choice, without being required.

pairs.key: [L136-Q1-2] Enforceable
pairs.value: Able to be legally upheld or required if not followed.

pairs.key: [L136-Q1-3] Aspirational
pairs.value: Expressing a hoped-for goal, without a firm requirement to achieve it.

quests.hint: Two of these describe whether a rule is required, and two describe whether it can actually be enforced or is just hoped for.
quests.explanation: Mandated and voluntary are opposites describing whether a rule is required or chosen. Enforceable and aspirational are different — both are about the weight a rule actually carries, one meaning it has real legal consequences, one meaning it's just a hoped-for goal.
quests.paragraphTopic: Vocabulary about the strength of a policy

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L136-Q2-0] The emissions cuts for large factories are mandated by federal law.
pairs.value: Big factories are legally required to reduce their emissions, under federal rules.

pairs.key: [L136-Q2-1] Smaller businesses are only asked to participate on a voluntary basis.
pairs.value: Smaller companies are simply invited to take part, without being required to.

pairs.key: [L136-Q2-2] The mandated targets are fully enforceable, with real penalties for violations.
pairs.value: The required goals for large factories carry genuine legal consequences if companies don't meet them.

pairs.key: [L136-Q2-3] The voluntary program's broader goal remains largely aspirational.
pairs.value: The wider aim of the optional program is mostly a hoped-for outcome, without any real requirement behind it.

quests.hint: Each sentence describes a different level of obligation in the same climate policy.
quests.explanation: The first sentence describes a legal requirement, and the second describes an optional alternative. The third confirms that the required part has real consequences, while the fourth is different — it describes the optional part's broader goal as mostly just hoped for.
quests.paragraphTopic: A climate policy's mix of rules and goals

quests.instruction: Match each version with its precise meaning.

pairs.key: [L136-Q3-0] Companies must reduce emissions by twenty percent by 2030.
pairs.value: Reducing emissions by twenty percent by 2030 is a legal requirement for companies.

pairs.key: [L136-Q3-1] Companies are encouraged to reduce emissions by twenty percent by 2030.
pairs.value: Reducing emissions by twenty percent by 2030 is a suggested goal for companies, not a legal requirement.

pairs.key: [L136-Q3-2] Companies hope to reduce emissions by twenty percent by 2030.
pairs.value: Reducing emissions by twenty percent by 2030 is an aspiration companies have expressed, without any binding commitment.

pairs.key: [L136-Q3-3] Companies have already reduced emissions by twenty percent.
pairs.value: Companies have already achieved a twenty percent reduction in emissions.

quests.hint: These four sentences look almost identical but differ in a small but important way — whether a goal is required, suggested, hoped for, or already achieved.
quests.explanation: The first states a legal requirement, must. The second softens that to encouragement, are encouraged to. The third describes only a hope, without any real commitment, hope to. The fourth is different from all three — it describes something already accomplished, in the past.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L137-Q1-0] Vision
pairs.value: A broad statement of what an organization hopes to become in the future.

pairs.key: [L137-Q1-1] Mission
pairs.value: A statement of an organization's core purpose and what it does now.

pairs.key: [L137-Q1-2] Values
pairs.value: The principles an organization believes should guide its behavior.

pairs.key: [L137-Q1-3] Target
pairs.value: A specific, measurable goal an organization aims to achieve.

quests.hint: These four words all describe different parts of a company's stated strategy.
quests.explanation: Vision and mission are related but different, one about a future hope, one about current purpose. Values and target are different — one describes guiding principles, one describes a specific, measurable goal.

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L137-Q2-0] The vision statement describes a future where clean energy is accessible to everyone.
pairs.value: The company's statement about the future imagines a world where clean energy is available to all.

pairs.key: [L137-Q2-1] The mission statement focuses on what the company actually does today: manufacturing solar panels.
pairs.value: The company's core-purpose statement is about its current, everyday work: making solar panels.

pairs.key: [L137-Q2-2] Its stated values emphasize sustainability and transparency.
pairs.value: The principles the company says it follows highlight caring for the environment and being open about its actions.

pairs.key: [L137-Q2-3] A specific target is to cut manufacturing waste by fifteen percent this year.
pairs.value: One concrete, measurable goal is reducing waste from manufacturing by fifteen percent within the year.

quests.hint: Each sentence describes a different part of the same company's stated strategy.
quests.explanation: The first sentence describes a future-looking vision, and the second describes the company's current, everyday mission. The third describes its guiding values, while the fourth is different — it describes one specific, measurable target.

quests.instruction: Match each statement with its type.

pairs.key: [L137-Q3-0] By 2040, we envision a world powered entirely by renewable energy.
pairs.value: This is a vision statement, describing a long-term hope for the future.

pairs.key: [L137-Q3-1] We design and manufacture affordable solar panels for homes and businesses.
pairs.value: This is a mission statement, describing what the company actually does.

pairs.key: [L137-Q3-2] We believe in honesty, even when it's inconvenient.
pairs.value: This is a values statement, describing a guiding principle.

pairs.key: [L137-Q3-3] We aim to open three new manufacturing facilities by the end of next year.
pairs.value: This is a target, describing a specific, measurable goal.

quests.hint: Each of these four statements belongs to a different category of company strategy.
quests.explanation: The first statement is a vision, describing a long-term hope. The second is a mission, describing current work. The third is a value, describing a guiding principle, while the fourth is a target, describing a specific, measurable goal.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L138-Q1-0] Sensational
pairs.value: Written to provoke strong excitement or shock, sometimes exaggerating.

pairs.key: [L138-Q1-1] Neutral
pairs.value: Free from strong emotional language or clear opinion.

pairs.key: [L138-Q1-2] Loaded
pairs.value: Containing words chosen to push the reader toward a particular judgment.

pairs.key: [L138-Q1-3] Even-handed
pairs.value: Presenting more than one side fairly, without favoring either.

quests.hint: Two of these describe emotionally charged language, and two describe more neutral or fair language.
quests.explanation: Sensational and loaded both use language to provoke a reaction, one through drama, one through word choice that nudges judgment. Neutral and even-handed are different — both avoid pushing the reader, one by avoiding strong language entirely, one by fairly representing more than one side.

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L138-Q2-0] 'City Officials Silent as Crisis Deepens' uses loaded language to suggest wrongdoing.
pairs.value: This headline's word choice implies officials are guilty of ignoring a worsening problem, even before any facts are given.

pairs.key: [L138-Q2-1] 'City Council Meeting Scheduled to Discuss Budget' is fairly neutral.
pairs.value: This headline simply states a fact, without pushing the reader toward any particular feeling about it.

pairs.key: [L138-Q2-2] 'Budget Disaster Could Bankrupt the City, Experts Warn' is more sensational.
pairs.value: This headline uses dramatic, alarming language that may exaggerate the actual severity of the issue.

pairs.key: [L138-Q2-3] The article itself takes a more even-handed approach, citing sources on multiple sides.
pairs.value: The actual article is more balanced than the headline, including views from more than one perspective.

quests.hint: Each sentence analyzes a different headline or article about the same city story.
quests.explanation: The first sentence analyzes a headline using loaded language, and the second analyzes a more neutral one. The third analyzes a more sensational headline, while the fourth is different — it shifts to describing the article itself, rather than a headline.
quests.paragraphTopic: Comparing a headline to its article

quests.instruction: Match each version with its precise meaning.

pairs.key: [L138-Q3-0] The headline claims the city is 'on the brink of collapse.'
pairs.value: The headline states, in dramatic terms, that the city is about to fail entirely.

pairs.key: [L138-Q3-1] The article states the city faces 'a significant but manageable budget gap.'
pairs.value: The article describes a real financial problem that is serious but still able to be handled.

pairs.key: [L138-Q3-2] The headline claims officials have 'refused to comment.'
pairs.value: The headline states that officials would not speak about the issue when asked.

pairs.key: [L138-Q3-3] The article notes officials 'were unavailable for comment before publication.'
pairs.value: The article explains that officials simply couldn't be reached in time, not that they refused to respond.

quests.hint: These four sentences look almost identical but differ in a small but important way — what the headline claims versus what the article actually says.
quests.explanation: The first is a dramatic headline claim. The second is the article's more measured version of a related but different point, the budget gap rather than the city itself. The third is another dramatic headline claim, about officials refusing comment. The fourth is different from all three — it's the article's more precise, less accusatory version of that same event.
quests.paragraphTopic: Precise paraphrasing of headline versus article claims

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L139-Q1-0] Symbolic
pairs.value: Representing something beyond its literal meaning.

pairs.key: [L139-Q1-1] Literal
pairs.value: Meaning exactly what the words say, without hidden meaning.

pairs.key: [L139-Q1-2] Ironic
pairs.value: Meaning the opposite of, or something quite different from, what is literally said.

pairs.key: [L139-Q1-3] Foreboding
pairs.value: Suggesting that something bad is about to happen.

quests.hint: Two of these describe how directly a text's meaning should be taken, in opposite directions. Two describe a meaning that reaches beyond the literal words.
quests.explanation: Literal and ironic are opposites, one meaning exactly what's said, one meaning something quite different. Symbolic and foreboding are different — both go beyond the literal meaning, one representing a deeper idea, one warning of trouble ahead.

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L139-Q2-0] The storm in the final chapter is often read symbolically, representing the character's inner turmoil.
pairs.value: Many readers interpret the storm at the end as standing for the character's emotional conflict, not just as actual weather.

pairs.key: [L139-Q2-1] Taken literally, it's simply a plot device that forces the characters indoors.
pairs.value: Read plainly, it's just a story event that brings the characters together in one place.

pairs.key: [L139-Q2-2] The narrator's cheerful description of the funeral is deeply ironic.
pairs.value: The narrator describing the funeral so happily actually suggests something quite different from real cheerfulness.

pairs.key: [L139-Q2-3] Earlier, a foreboding reference to 'dark clouds gathering' hints at what's to come.
pairs.value: An earlier mention of gathering dark clouds gives a subtle warning sign of trouble ahead.

quests.hint: Each sentence offers a different way of reading the same short story.
quests.explanation: The first sentence offers a symbolic reading, and the second offers the literal alternative to it. The third identifies an ironic moment, while the fourth is different — it identifies a foreboding hint elsewhere in the story.

quests.instruction: Match each line with how it should be read.

pairs.key: [L139-Q3-0] 'The sun always shines on her,' the narrator said, watching her funeral in the rain.
pairs.value: This line is ironic, since it describes sunshine while literally describing rain at a funeral.

pairs.key: [L139-Q3-1] 'Dark clouds gathered on the horizon as they set out.'
pairs.value: This line is foreboding, hinting that trouble lies ahead for the characters.

pairs.key: [L139-Q3-2] 'The house key rusted in the lock, and the paint peeled from the door.'
pairs.value: This line can be read literally, simply describing a neglected house.

pairs.key: [L139-Q3-3] 'The garden, once so full of life, had gone completely silent.'
pairs.value: This line is symbolic, suggesting a loss that goes beyond just the garden itself.

quests.hint: Each of these four lines calls for a different kind of literary reading.
quests.explanation: The first line is ironic, since cheerful words describe a sad, rainy scene. The second is foreboding, warning of trouble ahead. The third can be read literally, simply describing a neglected house, while the fourth is symbolic, suggesting a loss deeper than just the garden.
quests.paragraphTopic: Recognizing different kinds of literary meaning

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.key: [L140-Q1-0] Nuanced
pairs.value: Showing a careful understanding of subtle differences within a topic.

pairs.key: [L140-Q1-1] Oversimplified
pairs.value: Presented in a way that ignores important complexity.

pairs.key: [L140-Q1-2] Multifaceted
pairs.value: Having many different aspects or sides.

pairs.key: [L140-Q1-3] Reductive
pairs.value: Reducing something complex down to a single, overly simple explanation.

quests.hint: Two of these describe a genuinely complex understanding, and two describe an oversimplified one.
quests.explanation: Nuanced and multifaceted both describe a genuinely complex understanding, one careful about subtle differences, one aware of many sides. Oversimplified and reductive are different — both ignore real complexity, one broadly, one by boiling everything down to a single explanation.
quests.paragraphTopic: Vocabulary about complexity in an argument

quests.instruction: Match each sentence with what it means.

pairs.key: [L140-Q2-0] The issue is far more multifaceted than either side's talking points suggest.
pairs.value: The topic actually has many more sides to it than either group's simplified arguments admit.

pairs.key: [L140-Q2-1] One commentator offered a genuinely nuanced take, acknowledging both costs and benefits.
pairs.value: One writer gave a thoughtful, detailed analysis, recognizing both the downsides and the upsides.

pairs.key: [L140-Q2-2] Another reduced the entire debate to a single, reductive slogan.
pairs.value: A different writer boiled the whole complicated issue down to one overly simple catchphrase.

pairs.key: [L140-Q2-3] Readers seeking real understanding should be wary of oversimplified narratives on either side.
pairs.value: People who actually want to understand the issue should be cautious of overly simple stories from either side of the debate.

quests.hint: Each sentence makes a different point about how complex the same debate really is.
quests.explanation: The first sentence states that the issue is genuinely complex, and the second praises a writer who captured that complexity. The third criticizes a writer who oversimplified it, while the fourth is different — it offers general advice to readers about staying alert to oversimplification.
quests.paragraphTopic: Analyzing how complex a policy debate really is

quests.instruction: Match each version with its precise meaning.

pairs.key: [L140-Q3-0] This policy will fix the problem.
pairs.value: This claims the policy will completely solve the issue, with full confidence.

pairs.key: [L140-Q3-1] This policy might help with part of the problem.
pairs.value: This claims the policy could offer partial improvement, with real uncertainty about how much.

pairs.key: [L140-Q3-2] This policy has, in some cases, made the problem worse.
pairs.value: This claims the policy has actually had a harmful effect in certain specific situations.

pairs.key: [L140-Q3-3] This policy is unlikely to make any real difference.
pairs.value: This claims the policy probably won't have a meaningful effect either way.

quests.hint: These four sentences look almost identical but differ in a small but important way — how confidently and how completely each one claims the policy works.
quests.explanation: The first claims total success, will fix. The second claims only partial, uncertain help, might help with part. The third claims a specific, negative effect in certain cases, has made worse. The fourth is different from all three — it claims the policy probably won't matter either way.
quests.paragraphTopic: Precise paraphrasing of a policy's claimed effect
